content.text:
**Finding submitted: compliant** (confidence 0.86) — no redline proposed.

The fee architecture is genuinely usage- and order-based, which meets the MINCOMMIT **preferred** position rather than merely the fallback:

| Fee | Basis | Take-or-pay risk |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue share | % of revenue actually received, accrues at customer go-live | None |
| Implementation | T&M vs. agreed SOW, with NTE cap | None (cap favors us) |
| Maintenance/support | Annual, but continues only "provided that Corio continues to pay" | Effective exit |
| License / MarketSite access | Ordered service fees | Not volume-linked |

Two items I deliberately noted in the rationale rather than flagging, per the playbook's treatment of minor sub-elements:

1. **p0158's "minimum limitation of 40 Authorized Software Users per Customer"** is the only true "minimum" hit in the document, but it is a *metering convention inside a concession to us* — it governs how the royalty-free 3000-license pool is drawn down, not an obligation to purchase. Worth commercial awareness (it consumes the free pool faster for small customers) but not a rule breach.
2. **§4.4's "shortfall"** is a reciprocal audit true-up with a matching overpayment refund — exactly the mechanic the rule's redline guidance asks us to substitute *in place of* penalties, so it is already in the right shape and runs both ways.

The five-year initial term with no convenience termination (p0096) is the one structural feature worth mentioning, but it does not convert into a take-or-pay: because the substantial recurring spend is either usage-based or terminable-by-non-payment, we are not exposed to committed fees for volume we never use. I did not flag the term itself here, as term/renewal length belongs to a separate rule and flagging it under MINCOMMIT would double-count the same commercial term.
